craft.d: The largest structure humans have built in space, about 400 km up, with people living aboard without a break since November 2000.
China's space station, about 390 km up, crewed by taikonauts in rotations of about six months.
The Hubble Space Telescope, about 510 km up, has photographed the universe in visible, ultraviolet and near-infrared light since 1990.
NASA's X-ray observatory, on a long, stretched orbit reaching about a third of the way to the Moon.
ESA's X-ray observatory, on a stretched two-day orbit up to about 115,000 km from Earth.
NASA's gamma-ray telescope, about 530 km up, which maps the whole sky every three hours in the highest-energy light.
A NASA telescope that focuses high-energy X-rays, using a 10-metre mast unfolded in space, to study black holes and the remains of exploded stars.
NASA's planet hunter, on an orbit that swings out close to the Moon's distance every 13.7 days.
ESA's small telescope that measures the sizes of planets already found around nearby stars, about 700 km up.
Measures the polarisation of X-rays from black holes and neutron stars, about 600 km up; built by NASA with the Italian Space Agency.
A Japanese-led X-ray telescope, about 550 km up, that splits X-rays into very fine colours to measure the gas between galaxies.
A Chinese Academy of Sciences X-ray telescope, with ESA and Germany's Max Planck Institute as partners, that watches wide areas of sky for sudden X-ray flashes.
A French–Chinese satellite that catches gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe, and points its telescopes at them within minutes.
Maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, every six months, to study how the universe began and where the ingredients of life are found.

craft.t: Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer
craft.d: An ESA–Chinese Academy of Sciences mission that images how the solar wind strikes Earth's magnetic field, from a stretched orbit reaching far above the North Pole.
A small telescope that watches planets pass in front of their stars, to tell the planets' atmospheres apart from spots and flares on the stars.
The largest space telescope, seeing in infrared light, in a loop around the point L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth on the side away from the Sun.
ESA's telescope mapping billions of galaxies across a third of the sky, to study dark matter and dark energy, near L2.
NASA's wide-field infrared telescope, with a view a hundred times wider than Hubble's at the same sharpness, working near L2.
Has watched the Sun without a break from the point L1, 1.5 million km towards the Sun, since 1996, and has found more than 5,000 comets in its pictures.
Samples the solar wind at L1 about an hour before it reaches Earth, giving warning of space weather.
One of NASA's oldest working spacecraft, measuring the solar wind near L1 since 2004.
India's first solar observatory, in a loop around L1 since January 2024, watching the Sun's outer layers and the solar wind.
Studies the solar wind and the edge of the heliosphere, the bubble the Sun blows around the solar system, from L1.
Watches the whole sunlit face of Earth from L1, 1.5 million km towards the Sun (its EPIC camera), and measures the solar wind on its way to Earth.

craft.t: Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness 1 (formerly SWFO-L1)
craft.d: America's first satellite built only for space weather: from L1 it watches the solar wind and the Sun's eruptions (coronal mass ejections) heading for Earth, for NOAA's forecasters.
Photographs the geocorona, the faint ultraviolet glow of hydrogen at the very top of Earth's atmosphere, which reaches far out into space, from L1.
Flies through the Sun's outer atmosphere, closer to the Sun than any spacecraft before it: 6.1 million km from its surface at its closest, at about 690,000 km/h.
ESA's mission taking the closest pictures of the Sun and, as its orbit tilts, the first views of the Sun's poles.
Orbits the Sun slightly inside Earth's orbit, so it sees the Sun from a different angle and drifts slowly ahead of Earth.
Takes a picture of the whole Sun in ten colours of light every few seconds, from a high orbit over America; the source of most close-up pictures of the Sun.
Looks closely at the thin layer between the Sun's surface and its corona, where the Sun's atmosphere is heated to millions of degrees.
A Japanese solar observatory, built with NASA and the UK, studying the Sun's magnetic fields and the outbursts they cause.
Four identical spacecraft flying in a tight pyramid on a long loop around Earth, studying how magnetic fields snap and reconnect, the process behind auroras and solar flares.

craft.t: Time History of Events and Macroscale Interactions during Substorms (three craft)
craft.d: Three craft (A, D and E) on long loops around Earth, timing the bursts in Earth's magnetic field that make the aurora flare up.

craft.t: Thermosphere Ionosphere Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics
craft.d: Studies the upper atmosphere, 60 to 180 km up, and how the Sun heats and changes it.
The farthest human-made object, more than 25 billion km away, in interstellar space since 2012.
The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, in interstellar space since 2018.
Flew past Pluto in 2015 and the small, far world Arrokoth on 1 January 2019; now crossing the Kuiper belt.
Orbiting Jupiter since 2016 on long loops over its poles, studying its clouds, deep interior and magnetic field, and flying past its moons.
On its way to Jupiter's icy moon Europa, to find out whether the ocean under its ice could support life.
ESA's mission to Jupiter and three of its large moons, Ganymede, Callisto and Europa, to learn whether their buried oceans could support life.
On a twelve-year tour of the Trojan asteroids that share Jupiter's orbit, the first mission to visit them.
On its way to the metal-rich asteroid 16 Psyche, pushed by electric (ion) thrusters; it arrives in 2029.
As OSIRIS-REx it brought samples of the asteroid Bennu to Earth in 2023; renamed, it is on its way to the asteroid Apophis, which passes close to Earth in April 2029.
ESA's mission to the asteroid pair Didymos and Dimorphos, to measure what NASA's DART probe did when it struck Dimorphos in 2022: a test of moving an asteroid.
Two orbiters, ESA's and JAXA's, travelling together to Mercury; they separate once in orbit around it.
Brought samples of the asteroid Ryugu to Earth in 2020, then set off on an extended mission; it meets the small, fast-spinning asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031.
China's mission to collect samples from the small near-Earth asteroid Kamoʻoalewa, a possible piece of the Moon, and bring them to Earth, then go on to a comet.

craft.t: Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers
craft.d: One of two small identical spacecraft, Blue and Gold, built to study how the solar wind strips Mars's atmosphere, from two orbits at once.

craft.t: Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers
craft.d: The twin of ESCAPADE Blue.
Japan's mission to Mars's moons: it is to orbit Phobos, land, collect at least 10 g of its surface and bring the sample to Earth in 2031, the first return from the Mars system.
ESA's first mission to another planet, orbiting Mars since December 2003; its radar found signs of buried water ice.
The longest-working spacecraft at Mars, in orbit since October 2001; it mapped ice under the surface and relays messages from the rovers.
Orbiting Mars since 2006; its HiRISE camera can see objects the size of a kitchen table, and it relays data from the rovers.
Sniffs the thin Martian air for gases that could come from geology or life, and relays data from NASA's rovers.
The United Arab Emirates' first planetary mission, on a high orbit that shows the weather on the whole of Mars at once.
China's first Mars mission: its orbiter, still working, carried the Zhurong rover, which landed in May 2021.
A car-sized rover in Gale crater since August 2012, climbing Mount Sharp and reading its layers of rock like pages of Mars's history.
A rover in Jezero crater since February 2021, collecting rock samples in sealed tubes from an ancient river delta.
Mapping the Moon since 2009 in great detail, including the Apollo landing sites and the cold, dark craters near the poles.
India's lunar orbiter, mapping the Moon since 2019; it also relayed for Chandrayaan-3's lander, which touched down near the south pole in 2023.
Korea's first lunar mission, in orbit around the Moon since December 2022, carrying a NASA camera that looks into permanently shadowed craters.
Launched as one of five THEMIS craft studying the aurora, then sent to the Moon in 2011 with its twin P2; the pair measure the solar wind and Earth's magnetic tail around the Moon.
The twin of ARTEMIS P1, on a different orbit around the Moon, so the two measure the space around it at two places at once.
China's mission to the Moon's south pole, with an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a small hopping probe, to look for water ice in the shadowed craters.
NASA's first big Earth-watching satellite, measuring land, ocean, clouds and air since 2000.
Follows Earth's water: evaporation, clouds, rain, ice and snow.
Measures the ozone layer and air quality.
Part of the longest-running record of Earth's land from space, begun in 1972.
Works with Landsat 8 so that every place on land is pictured every eight days.
A radar satellite of the EU's Copernicus programme: it sees the ground through cloud and darkness.
Takes colour pictures of land and coasts for Copernicus, in 13 colours from blue to infrared.
Takes colour pictures of land and coasts for Copernicus; it went up on the last flight of the original Vega rocket.
Measures the oceans' height, temperature and colour for Copernicus.
Works with Sentinel-3A on the oceans' height, temperature and colour.
Maps the gases polluting the air every day.
Measures sea level to within a few centimetres, continuing a record begun in 1992.
Measures the thickness of sea ice and the ice sheets.
Measures the moisture in soil and the saltiness of the sea.
Studies how clouds and tiny particles in the air warm or cool the planet, with a radar and a laser.
The first space radar long enough in wavelength to see through forest canopies and weigh the world's forests.
A weather and climate satellite; its night-time camera shows city lights and fires.
One of the polar-orbiting satellites behind every weather forecast.
The newest of the polar-orbiting weather satellites.
The GOES-West weather satellite, 35,786 km up over the Pacific, where it keeps pace with Earth's turning.
The GOES-East weather satellite, 35,786 km up over the Americas; it also carries a coronagraph that watches the Sun.
Japan's weather satellite, 35,786 km up over the western Pacific.
Europe's newest-generation weather satellite (MTG-I1), 35,786 km up over Africa; it also detects lightning.
Surveys the height of nearly all water on Earth: oceans, lakes and rivers.
Sees the colour of the ocean in fine detail to track plankton, and the haze and clouds above it.
Measures carbon dioxide in the air around the world, and the faint glow plants give off as they grow.
Measures the height of the sea surface to a few centimetres, continuing a record of sea level that began in 1992.
The second of two identical sea-level satellites, following Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, to carry the sea-level record into the 2030s.
Measures the height of ice, sea, land and trees with a laser, 10,000 pulses a second.

craft.t: Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On
craft.d: Two satellites, one following the other about 220 km behind, that weigh moving water and ice by tiny changes in the distance between them.
The core of a fleet measuring rain and snow around the world every 30 minutes.
Maps the water in the top few centimetres of soil every few days.
A radar built by NASA and ISRO together that measures movements of land and ice of a centimetre or less.
The first of the US Space Force's new weather satellites, measuring winds over the ocean with a microwave imager; its orbit is published.
Part of NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet: from geostationary orbit, 36,000 km up, it passes messages between the ground and spacecraft below, such as the space station and Hubble.
Part of NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet: from geostationary orbit, 36,000 km up, it passes messages between the ground and spacecraft below, such as the space station and Hubble.

Part of NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet: from geostationary orbit, 36,000 km up, it passes messages between the ground and spacecraft below, such as the space station and Hubble.
Watched the Americas as GOES-East from 2017 to April 2025; now NOAA's spare in geostationary orbit, ready to take over if GOES-18 or GOES-19 fails.
Watched the Pacific as GOES-West from 2019 to 2023; now a second spare in geostationary orbit.
A European polar weather satellite whose soundings of temperature and moisture feed the world's weather forecasts.
The third of Europe's first-generation polar weather satellites, flying with Metop-B.
Japan's weather satellite over the western Pacific from 2015 to 2022; now the standby for Himawari-9.
